title: Peter by the fire (Mark 14:66–72)
hook: a servant girl, a denial, the rooster twice, and Peter breaks down weeping

segments.voice: Yesterday, a trial at night and two words, I am. Your line was silence can be strong.

While Jesus stands before the council upstairs, Mark cuts back to the courtyard below. Peter is there, the one who said earlier that same night, even if everyone else falls away, not I. When the others fled, he followed, at a distance, right into the high priest's courtyard. That took courage. He's sitting with the servants by a fire, warming himself. One of the high priest's servant girls walks past, stops, and really looks at him. You were with the Nazarene, she says. You were with Jesus. Not a soldier, not a judge: a young woman with a job to do, and one sentence.
screen: `MEANWHILE, THE COURTYARD.` → `A FIRE, AND PETER.` → `YOU WERE WITH JESUS.`

segments.voice: I don't know what you're talking about, Peter says, and he moves out to the gateway. A rooster crows. The girl sees him again and tells the people standing around: this is one of them. He denies it again. A little later the bystanders try: surely you're one of them, you're a Galilean; they can hear it in his accent. And Peter, in the King James Bible, "began to curse and to swear, saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak." Three denials, each one louder. Right then the rooster crows a second time, just as Jesus said: before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. Then Mark gives one short, plain sentence: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." The Greek behind when he thought thereon is rare and hard to pin down. Translators have guessed: he broke down, he threw himself down, he covered his head. Nobody is sure. But the verb for wept is clear, and its tense suggests he kept on weeping. Notice the timing. Upstairs, Jesus tells the truth, and it will cost him his life. Downstairs, Peter lies to save his. Mark sets them side by side. Tradition links Mark's gospel to Peter's own preaching; if so, Peter told this story on himself. He doesn't hide the failure. The weeping is where he starts again. This week went from perfume, to the upper room, to a garden where he prayed abba, to a kiss, a trial, and now a fire.
screen: `THE SERVANT GIRL.` · `THREE DENIALS, LOUDER EACH TIME.` · `THE ROOSTER CROWS TWICE.` · `WHEN HE THOUGHT THEREON, HE WEPT.` · then, large: `I KNOW NOT THIS MAN.`

segments.voice: Think of a time you let someone down, or let yourself down, something real but manageable, not the worst thing you've ever done, and instead of explaining it away, let yourself feel sorry for it; if tears come, let them. Sadness isn't the end of the story: for Peter, it was the turning point. If you pray, you can bring that failure to God as it is.
Peter, warming himself by the fire while three denials slip out, and a rooster crows twice. Then he breaks down weeping.
Your line: he wept. And the story didn't stop there. Day two hundred twenty-four closes the week.

howItsDone: Christians read Peter's denial in Holy Week, and a rooster became a common symbol of Peter and of repentance, carved on church towers and pictured in art of his weeping.

fork.reveal: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." Mark keeps Peter's failure in, and Christians often see it as the start of his turning back.

chat.says: Peter denied Jesus three times. Why does that story matter so much?
options: He failed, wept, and didn't hide it; the weeping is where he began again.
It shows Peter never really loved Jesus in the first place.
It shows that one failure like that ends a person's place for good.
chat.meaning: And when he thought thereon, he wept. Peter didn't hide the failure; for him, sadness was the turning point.

Galilean.meaning: someone from Galilee; Peter's accent gave him away

high priest.meaning: the chief priest, whose courtyard Peter sat in

abba.meaning: Aramaic for father; Jesus's word in the garden
